## Part 1: Restaurant Health Inspections (25 points)

The first dataset contains restaurant health inspection scores from Montgomery County. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv`

The dataset includes the name of the establishment, the number of points for critical and non-critical areas, the total points, maximum points possible, the compliance score, and the grade.

### Task 1: Read the data (2 points)

```{r}
Restaurant_Health_Inspections <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv")
```

### Task 2: Calculate the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of compliance scores. Save the results in a new dataframe called `compliance_stats`. (6 points)

```{r}
compliance_stats <- Restaurant_Health_Inspections |> summarize(mean_compliance = mean(compliance_score), sd_compliance = sd(compliance_score), min_compliance = min(compliance_score), max_compliance = max(compliance_score))
```

### Task 3: Create a histogram of the compliance scores with a vertical line showing the mean. Include a headline and label the x and y axes. (8 points)

```{r}
Restaurant_Health_Inspections |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(aes(x = compliance_score), binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score) - sd(compliance_score)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score) + sd(compliance_score)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +   labs(title = "Distribution of Restaurant Health Inspection Compliance Scores from Montgomery County.", x = "Compliance Scores", y = "Number of Observations")

```

### Task 4: Write 2–3 sentences interpreting what the standard deviation and histogram tell us about the distribution of compliance scores. What would be newsworthy about this distribution? What's the story here? (9 points)

The stadard deviation tells us that the distribution deviates largly from the mean. There is a large spread from a minimun of 42 to a maximum of 100, with the mean being a score of about 96. The histogram shows a large left skew. Although there is a large amount of high compliance scores, there are some low scores skewing the data. Therefore, the low scores would be newsworthy for this distribution. The story could be comparing the high 100 compliance scores, to very low scores that deviate from the mean. The story could investigate why these scores are so low and what health protocals these restaurant violate.

## Part 2: Daily Transit Ridership — Z-Scores (30 points)

Your editor wants you to identify unusual days in WMATA's daily ridership data that might be worth investigating as story leads. The dataset contains daily bus and rail totals, along with the day of the week. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv`

### Task 5: Load the WMATA ridership data. (2 points)

```{r}
WMATA_ridership_date <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv")
```

### Task 6: Using `mutate()`, add a column called `rail_zscore` that is the z-score for rail ridership, calculated using the overall mean and standard deviation of all days. Save the result as `wmata_zscores`. (7 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores <- WMATA_ridership_date |> mutate(mean_rail = mean(rail),sd_rail = sd(rail), rail_zscore = (total - mean_rail) / sd_rail)
```

### Task 7: Rail ridership varies a lot by day of the week. Using `group_by()` and `mutate()`, add a column called `weekday_zscore` that calculates each day's rail z-score relative to other days with the same `weekday` (for example, a Sunday compared to other Sundays). Remember to `ungroup()` and save the result back to `wmata_zscores`. (8 points)

```{r}
  wmata_zscores <- wmata_zscores |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  mutate(
    dow_mean = mean(rail),
    dow_sd = sd(rail),
    weekday_zscore = (total - dow_mean) / dow_sd
  ) |>
  ungroup()

```

### Task 8: Filter for days where the absolute value of `rail_zscore` is greater than 2, and separately for days where the absolute value of `weekday_zscore` is greater than 2. Arrange each so the most extreme days appear first. How many unusual days does each method find? (5 points)

```{r}
unusual_rail_day <- wmata_zscores |>
  filter(abs(rail_zscore) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(rail_zscore)))

unusual_weekday <- wmata_zscores |>
  filter(abs(weekday_zscore) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(weekday_zscore)))


```

There are 427 observations for unusual days where the absolute value of `rail_zscore` is greater than 2. There are 595 observatons where the absolute value of `weekday_zscore` is greater than 2. 

### Task 9: Write 2–3 sentences: How do the two lists of unusual days differ, and what story leads does each suggest? (8 points)

The two lists of unusual days differ because the highest weekday_zscore is greater than the highest rail_zscore by 4. The highest weekday_zscore was 8.31 on Friday, March 28, 2025. The highest rail_zscore was 4.83 on Tuesday, March 31, 2026. For the weekday_zscores that are greater than 2, there are 595 observations. This suggests a story lead on the high volume of weekend ridership. This story could look at what and who this impacts, as well as environmental concerns from the vast use of the WMATA on the weekend. For the rail_zscore that are greater than 2, there are 427 observations. The top 14 z-scores for this list are all on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. This suggests a story lead on the high rail use during these three days. The story could look at rail ridership is high during these dates and what the benefits of riding the WMATA railway were as opposed to the bus.

## Part 3: Maryland Car Theft Rates (25 points)

Your editor has assigned you a story about car thefts in Maryland and wants you to find out which counties have the highest rates and which saw the biggest changes. The dataset contains car theft counts for Maryland counties in 2023 and 2024 along with population figures. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv`

### Task 10: Load the car thefts data. (2 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv")
```

### Task 11: Using `mutate()`, add two columns: `theft_rate`, the 2024 car theft rate per 10,000 residents, and `pct_change`, the percent change in thefts from 2023 to 2024. Save the result back to `md_car_thefts`. (10 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts |> mutate(theft_rate = thefts_2023/population * 10000, pct_change = ((thefts_2024 - thefts_2023) / thefts_2023) * 100)
```


### Task 12: Show the five counties with the highest 2024 theft rate, the five with the largest percent increase, and the five with the largest percent decrease. (5 points)

```{r}


md_car_thefts |> 
  summarize(IQR = IQR(thefts_2024))

md_car_thefts |> 
  mutate(thefts_percentile = ntile(thefts_2024, 100))

```

### Task 13: Write 2–3 sentences describing what these calculations reveal about car thefts in Maryland. What is the lede of a story based on your findings? (8 points)

These calculations reveal that Baltimore City and Prince George's County both have some of the highest theft rates out of the Maryland car thefts data. Therefore the lede of a story based on my findings would be: Despite a decrease in theft rates from 2023 to 2024 in Baltimore City and Prince George's County, both areas have the highest car theft rate in 2024 in Maryland.

## Part 4: Data Analysis Scenario (20 points)

A county parks department releases data showing that its 12 community swimming pools average 187 visitors per day during the summer season, with a standard deviation of 42 visitors across the pools' average daily attendance. Your editor suspects that a handful of pools are dramatically underperforming and wants a story. You also learn that the department's figures are based on a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than a complete count.

Write 4–5 sentences for each of the following questions:

### Question A: How would you use descriptive statistics and z-scores to identify which pools are genuinely underperforming, and why is that more useful than simply ranking pools by raw attendance? (10 points)

You can use descriptive statistics and z-scores to identify which pools are genuinely underperforming by calculating the z-score of each daily attendance for each pool. This will indicate how far the average daily attendance deviates from the actual mean. This will help to demonstrate which pools are true outliers, rather than just ranking them. Therefore, this is more useful than simply ranking the pools by attendance because this does not demonstrate how far away the attendance is from the mean. This creates a consistant or standardized way to determine which pools are genuinely underperforming.

### Question B: The department collected its attendance figures using a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than tracking every day. What questions would you ask about the sample before relying on these figures for a story? What concerns would you raise in your story? (10 points)

A qestions I would ask about the sample before relying on these figures for a story would be: How were these specific 60 days per pool determined? What are these specific 60 days? How was the attendance actually tracked? Concerns that I would raise in my story are how outliers are determined from this 60 day sample. Another concern I would have is because this is a random 60 day sample, weather could impact this. I would be concerned about if this gives an accurate representation of when people truly attend the pool, because we do not know the seasonal pattern. Although summer is usually always hot, seasonal inconsistencies could have occurred.
